page: Google Cloud Platform n4-standard-4 is a general-purpose virtual machine belonging to the n4 server family. It features 4 vCPUs mapped to 2 physical Intel cores with hyper-threading enabled, providing 2 threads per core. The instance is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding a balanced 4.0 GB of RAM per core. It operates on the x86_64 architecture and includes a dedicated CPU allocation. The processor cache architecture consists of 48 KB L1d cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and a large 260 MB L3 cache. This instance does not include local storage or bundled GPUs.

Performance benchmarks reveal a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core capabilities. The server demonstrates average performance in single-core tasks, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1561.99 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1807.0. However, multi-core performance is categorized as weak, as evidenced by a stress-ng multi-core score of 3213.05 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 4100.0. Memory bandwidth is also a limiting factor, with uncached read and write speeds of 32.36 GB/sec and 21.01 GB/sec respectively, both falling into the weak category.

Despite memory and multi-core constraints, the Intel processor supports advanced instruction sets, including AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX_TILE and AMX_INT8) for matrix operations. These instructions assist in workloads like cryptography, where the Passmark CPU encryption test achieves an average rating. The instance also handles single-threaded compression and decompression moderately well, with gzip compression reaching 28.23 GB/sec. Static web serving throughput is also average at 6.53 GB/sec.

Given its hardware profile and benchmark results, the n4-standard-4 is suited for workloads that do not demand high multi-threaded throughput or intensive memory bandwidth. Appropriate applications include basic web serving, single-threaded text processing, and lightweight utility tasks. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the instance provides a standard resource density for general-purpose computing, though users requiring high-performance database operations or software compilation may face performance bottlenecks due to weak multi-core and memory subsystem benchmarks.
